about: Questions and answers: for every guest answer of 30 or more words, gpt-6.1-sol (medium effort) wrote interview-style questions about how the guest understands an entity or event. Only questions whose answer shows judgment or taste were kept, each asks one thing and stands alone, and each answer is the guest's own reply, synthesized from the transcript (rewritten in the first person, filler removed, fragments joined). Every supporting quote was checked word for word against the transcript.
Categories are assigned per guest by hand from each question and answer; each question has exactly one.

Rubrics: the same v10 rubric writer as the raw-transcript evaluation (here run with gpt-6.1-sol at medium effort) turned each guest answer into one-idea criteria. One answer produced no rubrics and is unscored.

Answers: each model saw a one-line host introduction naming the guest, then the question, and answered as the guest at xhigh effort with no browsing or tools. Claude models ran through claude -p; GPT models through codex exec.
Judge: gpt-6-luna at high effort with the same core-criterion prompt as the raw-transcript evaluation (which used gpt-5.6-luna). The guest's answer is withheld from the judge.

Caveats: Claude answers ran much longer than GPT answers (median 213 to 453 words versus 68 to 152), and longer answers have more chances to cover a rubric. Haiku 5.5 declined 4 of the 56 questions, saying it would not invent first-person speech for a real person; declines count as misses.
Scores measure coverage of the ideas in the guest's actual answer, not overall answer quality. ASR and speaker labels may contain errors.

items.question: How do you understand the apparent performance gap between convolutional networks and vision transformers through your work on “A ConvNet for the 2020s”?
items.object: The performance gap between convolutional networks and vision transformers
items.reference: So that was a really interesting story. We were working on this paper in 2021, and back then, transformers had just entered the computer vision research space through the introduction of vision transformers, right? And then everybody from the vision community had been switching to vision transformers from more traditional convnets, and they were getting better and better performance. So in this work, we wanted to investigate whether truly convnets had lost their competitiveness, and whether it's possible to control all the design components to study whether convnets can be modernized to be on par with vision transformers at that time. We wanted to study whether the seeming performance gap between vision transformers and convnets is due to their inherent design, like whether you use self-attention or convolution, or due to other seemingly small design details. And we found the answer to be the latter. So after a lot of studying, of modernizing the design components of a convnet, we eventually got the model to be on par with very strong vision transformers at that time on a diverse range of tasks. So this demonstrates that no matter whether you choose convnets or vision transformers, as long as you get everything correct, you'll get the same frontier-level performance on vision tasks.

items.question: How do you assess the importance of neural network architecture choice for making AI more useful?
items.object: Neural network architecture choice and its practical importance
items.reference:
I largely tend to agree, but I wouldn't say it doesn't matter. I would say, as long as you get everything correct, as long as you explore the design space enough, you'll converge to some point where it's kind of the Pareto frontier in terms of accuracy and efficiency trade-off. And it's very hard to go off this frontier. I think in the past many years, there haven't been innovations that have been widely adopted other than the mature architectures that we already were working with several years ago.

I do think, from a practical point of view, what data we train the model on matters more than the architecture choice. As long as the input/output interface stays the same, architecture is how we parameterize the function approximator, right? The very basic function of neural networks or deep learning. As long as you get a few things correct, like using residual connections, using self-attention or other reasonable mechanisms, and having the right activation at the right places, feed forward layers at the right places, you'll be very close or at the frontier curve of this performance versus efficiency balance.

items.question: How do you assess whether internet-scale computer vision datasets are broad enough to support models that generalize to every task?
items.object: The breadth of internet-scale computer vision datasets
items.reference:
So I will first talk a little bit about the context. This paper is more vision-focused. Over years, people have been developing larger and larger datasets, from more and more diverse sources. Initially we had MNIST, and then CIFAR, and then ImageNet, and then internet-scale datasets like DataCamp or Conceptual Captions, CC, from Google. They have seemingly more and more diverse images, and they are larger and larger, from tens of thousands to billion scale. It was kind of tempting to make the assumption that we are already good with datasets because it's really all the things you can get from the internet. But in some of our initial experiments, we found that these datasets are still nothing like each other.

We designed a very dumb experiment that doesn't make sense at all as a deep learning training program. Given three very large-scale computer vision datasets, we train a neural network to classify which dataset a particular image comes from. It's not a practical problem; it's just to try to guess the dataset's origin. It's a multiclass classification problem. It turns out, even with these seemingly very diverse datasets, the model can still tell this answer with surprisingly high accuracy, higher than 80% when you have three datasets. The random guessing accuracy would be 33%, but the model can be much better than that. So this means, to a model, these datasets are still very, very different. It has very clear cues to tell which dataset this image comes from. Of course, we are doing this on held-out validation sets. We are not predicting the training images.

But still, this has been surprisingly accurate, and that prompts us to reflect: have we really been successful in curating a large-scale, all-encompassing dataset, at least in the computer vision domain? What kind of dataset is the end goal? It's kind of hard to define this so-called all-encompassing global distribution dataset. Different people might have different criteria, and it might not be a reasonable assumption there.

A big story of the success of LM is that it's not a domain-specific model, right? We want the model to be able to do everything, and a common assumption is that we need the model to have seen everything during training. How much progress are we making on that? It seems from this initial experiment that we haven't reached that point yet, and it still makes sense to think about how we curate these datasets for the model to be really generalizing to every task we want the model to be good at.
